name: Barolo

climate.koppen_name: Temperate, no dry season, hot summer

climate: Seasons this warm ripen Dolcetto, Nebbiolo, Sémillon, Cabernet Franc and Tempranillo fully without cooking off their freshness.
Nebbiolo and Dolcetto sit in their sweet spot, so the wines can show the style they are known for.
Rain picks up at harvest. Growers race to pick before rot sets in, and vintages vary more.

soil.rock: Limestone makes alkaline soil that drains well yet can hold water for the vines. It is usually planted to grapes valued for their acidity.
soil.top: The topsoil holds water well and drains at a steady pace, so vines rarely go thirsty or sit in wet ground. Its high pH can starve vines of iron and yellow the leaves, so growers plant lime-tolerant rootstocks.

land: The high ground runs about 2°F cooler than the low ground. Higher vineyards ripen later and keep more acidity, so one grape can make lighter or richer wine here depending on height.
Much of it is steep. Cold air and rain run off, so frost and waterlogging are rare and soils stay thin, keeping yields low. Steep rows are slow and costly to work, often by hand.

winkler: Good for generous crops of standard to good wine.

sheet.place: Barolo is 100% Nebbiolo from hills just south of Alba, in 11 communes. It must age at least 38 months, 18 of them in wood, and Riserva needs 62.

claims.claim: Barolo is made from Nebbiolo only. The disciplinare allows no other grape.

The DOCG zone covers all of Barolo, Castiglione Falletto and Serralunga d'Alba, and parts of eight more communes: Monforte d'Alba, Novello, La Morra, Verduno, Grinzane Cavour, Diano d'Alba, Cherasco and Roddi. That makes 11 communes, all in the province of Cuneo.
The five original core communes (Barolo, Castiglione Falletto, Serralunga d'Alba, Monforte d'Alba and La Morra) are said to make over 87% of the wine.
The zone sits just south of Alba in the Langhe hills, above the Tanaro river.
Vines must be on clay and limestone soils, or a mix of the two. Valley floors, damp flat land and poorly sunlit ground are excluded.
The disciplinare says most of the zone is Tortonian soil, made of layered marls and sands. The marls are grey-blue and not very hard. They form low, rounded, whitish hills.

The disciplinare dates the Langhe soils to the Tortonian and Messinian ages, about 7 million years ago, as the Padano sea withdrew. It describes limestone and tufa layers with gypsum and minerals in some areas.
Western communes are on Tortonian soil. La Morra and Barolo are the examples. It is calcareous marl, more compact and fertile than the eastern soil.
Eastern communes are on older Helvetian (also called Serravallian) soil. Serralunga d'Alba and Monforte d'Alba are the examples. It is sandstone-based, compact and less fertile.
Castiglione Falletto has mixed soils with a good share of sand. It sits between the two formations.
Cannubi (Barolo commune) and Ravera (Novello) are named as vineyards on or near the border between the two soil types.
Wines from La Morra and Barolo tend to be lighter and more perfumed. Wines from Serralunga, Monforte and Castiglione Falletto tend to be bolder and firmer. Exposure and vine age cause exceptions.
Vineyards must lie between 170 m and 540 m above sea level.
The commune of Barolo itself ranges from 213 m to 480 m. The village is at 305 m, on a small spur-shaped plateau ringed by hills.
The Barolo zone is about 50 m higher than the Barbaresco zone. Serralunga d'Alba sits on one of the highest hilltops.
Exposure is not fixed, but new plantings may not face north (roughly -45 to +45 degrees). Vines must be on hills, trained on Guyot, at least 3,500 vines per hectare for new plantings.
The climate is continental, moderated by the Tanaro river and its tributaries. Harvest usually falls in early to mid October. The main risks are rain, downy mildew and spring hail.
Nebbiolo is picked late, often among foggy hills.

Barolo needs at least 38 months of aging counted from 1 November of the harvest year. At least 18 of those months must be in wood. It cannot be sold before 1 January of the fourth year after the harvest.

Barolo Riserva needs at least 62 months from 1 November of the harvest year, with at least 18 in wood. Release is from 1 January of the sixth year after harvest. The producer asks for the Riserva label after the aging time has passed.
Some sources give the rule as three years total with 18 months in barrel, and Riserva as five years.

Grape yield is capped at 8 tonnes per hectare, or 7.2 t/ha when a Menzione Geografica Aggiuntiva with 'vigna' is used. Wine yield is capped at 70% of the grapes, 56 hl/ha. Grapes must reach 12.5% natural alcohol (13.0% for MGA with 'vigna').
The finished wine must be garnet red, dry, full and harmonious, with at least 13.0% alcohol, 4.5 g/l total acidity and 22.0 g/l extract.
Vinification and aging must happen inside the delimited zone. The Ministry can allow it in the whole territory of some neighbouring communes.
Bottles must be Albeisa-shaped or traditional, in dark glass. Barolo chinato, a flavoured wine, is allowed on a Barolo base.
Barolo DOCG wines carry the vintage year on the label. The disciplinare says Barolo is known for wines that are harmonious, structured and long-lived.
Barolo became a DOC by decree of 23 April 1966 and a DOCG by decree of 1 July 1980 (Gazzetta Ufficiale 22 January 1981).
The disciplinare credits Camillo Benso, Count of Cavour, and Giulia Colbert Falletti, the last Marchesa di Barolo, with starting a rich, harmonious style of Barolo in the mid 1800s.
The zone was first demarcated in 1896. Grinzane Cavour and parts of Novello and Verduno were added in 1909. Parts of Cherasco, Diano d'Alba and Roddi came with the 1966 DOC.

Menzioni Geografiche Aggiuntive (MGA) are named vineyard areas or commune designations that can follow the word Barolo on the label. The disciplinare lists them in Article 8 and defines their borders in an annex.
The Barolo MGA were introduced in 2010. Barbaresco did the same in 2007. In total 181 were delimited: 170 vineyard areas and 11 village designations.

The 'vigna' mention (a named single plot) can only be added after an MGA. It needs separate vinification and storage, the producer must make and bottle the wine, and the type must be no more than half the size of the word Barolo.
The wine is named after the town and castle of Barolo.

The village's own name is of uncertain origin. The most repeated theory is Celtic 'bas reul', meaning 'low place'. Another links it to a Celtic word for river, referring to the Tanaro. Early records show 'Villa Barogly' around 1200. Piedmontese is Bareul.
The word Langhe may come from 'lingue', tongues of land, according to some scholars.
